problems.title: The feature compensation rescales the target mean instead of restoring it
problems.source_location: Section 3.3, PDF pp. 5–6; released CLIP/inversion/cont_model.py, contrastive_selection.
claim: Section 3.3, PDF pp. 5–6, motivates alignment of synthetic and real features. Released CLIP/inversion/cont_model.py, contrastive_selection, lines 177–188, and the corresponding ResNet compensation around lines 545–556 target a prescribed mean \(\mu\) and standard deviation \(\sigma\). For selected mean \(\bar z\) and standard deviation \(s\), they use \(b=\mu-\bar z\), \(a=\sigma/(s+10^{-8})\), and \(z_i^{\rm code}=(z_i+b)a\).
analysis: The mean of that expression is \((\bar z+\mu-\bar z)a=\mu a\), rather than \(\mu\). For selected features \((10,18,26)\), mean \(18\), sample standard deviation \(8\), and targets \(\mu=10\), \(\sigma=4\), the result is approximately \((1,5,9)\), with mean \(5\) and standard deviation \(4\). Centering first and restoring the mean after scaling gives \((6,10,14)\). The stabilizing epsilon changes the approximation slightly but not the mean-restoration defect.
result: The compensation’s empirical mean is algebraically wrong for nonzero target mean and nonunit scale, but downstream accuracy effects and publication-run lineage are not established.
repair: Center the selected sample, rescale its residuals, and add the target mean after scaling. Any reported finite implementation checks are historical; benchmark effects are unmeasured.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.
problems.impact_rationale: The compensation’s empirical mean is algebraically wrong for nonzero target mean and nonunit scale, but downstream accuracy effects and publication-run lineage are not established.
problems.existing_correction_status: The existing local proposal is retained; no author correction of the cited current formula or release path was identified.

problems.title: The contrastive loss, selection ranking, and temperature explanation use different objectives
problems.source_location: Section 3.3, Eq. (6), PDF p. 6; Algorithm 2; Appendix D.3, Eq. (28), PDF p. 21; current CLIP/inversion/cont_model.py, lines 54–79.
claim: Section 3.3, PDF p. 6, Eq. (6), defines the negative contrastive objective as

The prose selects by mean cosine similarity, the named equation uses log-mean-exponentiated similarity, and Appendix D.3 argues that temperature does not change rankings. The current selection code uses the former, while its training code includes self-pairs excluded in the equation.
analysis: For selected unit vectors \(e_1,e_2\), choose unit candidates \(A=(0.7,-0.7,\sqrt{0.02})\) and \(B=(0.1,0.1,\sqrt{0.98})\). Their mean cosines are \(0\) and \(0.1\), while their log-mean-exponential scores are \(\log\cosh(0.7/T)\) and \(0.1/T\). The first exceeds the second at \(T=1\), but is smaller for sufficiently large \(T\). Mean cosine, log-mean-exponential and diagonal-inclusive objectives therefore need not induce the same ranking.

At \(T=1\), the log-mean-exponential scores are \(0.2272702294\) for \(A\) and \(0.1\) for \(B\); at \(T=4\), they are \(0.0152349749\) and \(0.025\), reversing the preferred candidate. For two orthogonal unit features, diagonal-excluded loss is \(0\), while the current diagonal-inclusive loss is \(\log((e+1)/2)\approx0.6201145070\). These are distinct objectives, not a universal additive shift.
result: Valid unit-vector examples reverse the stated rankings and expose different self-pair treatment; the method’s empirical benefit is not disproved.

The current contrastive training function additionally constructs Adam, whereas the paper’s contrastive-MLP protocol specifies SGD. This protocol discrepancy is retained without assigning a measured benchmark effect.
repair: Either implement log-mean-exp selection with self-exclusion in training and acknowledge temperature-dependent ranking, or explicitly distinguish the existing mean-cosine selection from a self-including training objective. Choosing the intended alternative requires author intent and experimental provenance.
problems.impact_rationale: Valid unit-vector examples reverse the stated rankings and expose different self-pair treatment; the method’s empirical benefit is not disproved.

problems.title: A real-data evidence density is not constant under a changing synthetic marginal
problems.source_location: Eq. (3), PDF p. 4; Appendix B, Eq. (19), PDF p. 16; full-model objective Eqs. (5)/(22), PDF pp. 5/17.
claim: Eq. (3), PDF p. 4, and its detailed derivation in Appendix B, Eq. (19), PDF p. 16, use Bayes’ rule to obtain

\[ \begin{aligned} D_{\rm KL}(p_s(o_{l-1}\mid o_l)\Vert p_r(o_{l-1}\mid o_l)) ={}&D_{\rm KL}(p_s(o_{l-1}\mid o_l)\Vert p_r(o_{l-1}))\\ &-\mathbb E_{p_s(o_{l-1}\mid o_l)}\log p_r(o_l\mid o_{l-1}) +\log p_r(o_l). \end{aligned} \]
analysis: An evidence density can be constant with respect to parameters in a frozen-target PMI subproblem yet depend on the synthetic marginal when that distribution changes. Dropping it is justified only for the former optimization. The following two-state construction addresses the latter scope, not every frozen-layer update.

Let one deterministic identity layer act on \(\{0,1\}\), with real marginal \(r=(0.9,0.1)\) and positive synthetic marginal \(q\). The original joint objective is \(D_{\rm KL}(q\Vert r)\), minimized at \(q=r\). The inverse-conditionals are identical point masses, so their prior term \(-\log r_z\) cancels evidence \(+\log r_z\). Dropping the averaged evidence leaves \[\widetilde J(q)=\sum_zq_z\log q_z-2\sum_zq_z\log r_z,\] whose minimizer is \(q_z\propto r_z^2\), namely \[(0.9878048780,0.0121951220)\]. This differs from \(r\) even though the conditional-independence approximation is exact. The later Gaussian surrogate and fixed-target PMI subproblem are not disproved by this discrete diagnostic.
result: Supported derivation-scope qualification; no universal claim that the complete continual-learning method fails is established.
repair: For a theoretical joint objective, retain the full averaged evidence term, or explicitly state and enforce a fixed marginal over the targets. Restoring it in this example cancels the spurious cross-entropy contribution and recovers \(D_{\rm KL}(q\Vert r)\), with minimizer \(q=r\). That restoration follows exactly from Bayes’ rule and the displayed calculation.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.
problems.impact_rationale: The variable-marginal expectation is not constant, but its omission is valid for frozen targets; the finding narrows the joint-KL interpretation of an explicitly approximate practical surrogate.
problems.existing_correction_status: The existing local proposal is retained; no author correction of the cited current formula or release path was identified.

impact_rationale: The current release miscenters selected features and implements different contrastive rankings/self-pair conventions; the KL concern concerns changing-target surrogate interpretation. No continual-learning accuracy reversal or central impossibility result is established.
